FP32, FP16 and BF16 bit layouts
COMP7608B · Lecture 2 Q02
NVIDIA, reduced-precision formats
Sign sets polarity. Exponent sets range. Fraction sets precision.
FP32 s e e e e e e e e f f f f f f f f f f f f f f f f f f f f f f f
32 bits = 1 sign + 8 exponent + 23 fraction
FP16 s e e e e e f f f f f f f f f f
16 bits = 1 sign + 5 exponent + 10 fraction
More fraction bits than BF16
BF16 s e e e e e e e e f f f f f f f
16 bits = 1 sign + 8 exponent + 7 fraction
Same exponent width as FP32
Both 16-bit formats halve FP32 storage. BF16 keeps a wider range, while FP16 keeps finer 
precision.

QUANTIZATION
Error accumulation and mixed precision
COMP7608B · Lecture 2 18
Start at 2048. Add 1 four times. The exact answer is 2052.
Accumulator After +1 After +1 After +1 After +1 Final error
FP32 reference 2049 2050 2051 2052 0
FP16 each step 2048 2048 2048 2048 4
FP16 inputs, FP32 sum 2049 2050 2051 2052 0
At 2048, FP16 spacing is 2. Each 2048 + 1 rounds back to 2048.
Use higher precision for sums, normalization and softmax to limit further error.
Upcasting cannot recover bits already lost. Storage and computation can use different precisions.
Quantized models already mix formats
Qwen2-7B-Instruct-AWQ INT4 linear weights with FP16 activations.
Qwen3-30B-A3B-FP8 FP8 weights, with routers and LM head kept in BF16.
Toy sequential sum, round-to-nearest-even. Actual accumulation depends on the kernel. Sources: NVIDIA accuracy guidance and the named model configs.

QUANTIZATION
Post-training quantization and QAT
COMP7608B · Lecture 2 Q09
PyTorch, Quantization-Aware Training for LLMs /   Frantar et al., GPTQ /   Lin et al., AWQ
Post-training quantization (PTQ)
A trained checkpoint is already available. Quantize it using weight statistics
and, for methods such as GPTQ or AWQ, representative calibration inputs.
Checkpoint Calibration + conversion Quantized checkpoint
Quantization-aware training (QAT)
Simulate quantize + dequantize in the forward pass, then update weights
with gradients. Export real low-bit weights after training or fine-tuning.
Rounding uses an approximate backward gradient, often a straight-through estimator.
PTQ is a low-cost first deployment candidate. QAT adds training cost to help recover quality.

concepts.title: Floating-point layouts and precision-range tradeoffs
concepts.summary: Floating-point formats encode sign, exponent, and fraction: sign gives polarity, exponent controls range, and fraction controls precision. FP32 uses 1/8/23 bits; FP16 uses 1/5/10; BF16 uses 1/8/7. Both 16-bit formats halve FP32 storage, but BF16 retains FP32's exponent width while FP16 has more fraction bits. For the shown value 6.5078125, BF16 rounds to 6.5 with absolute error 0.0078125 (about 0.12%), while FP16 represents that particular value exactly.

sources.quote: Sign sets polarity. Exponent sets range. Fraction sets precision. ... Both 16-bit formats halve FP32 storage. BF16 keeps a wider range, while FP16 keeps finer precision.
The same value in FP32 and BF16 x = 6.5078125 ... BF16 stores 6.5. Absolute error = 0.0078125, or about 0.12% of the original value. Round to nearest. FP16 represents this particular value exactly.

concepts.title: Quantization and reconstruction with scale and zero-point
concepts.summary: Affine quantization maps a real value x to an integer code using q = clip(round(x / s) + z, qmin, qmax), then reconstructs it as x̂ = s × (q − z). Here s > 0 is the step size, z is the integer code representing zero, and clipping keeps the rounded code within the selected integer range. The reconstructed value approximates the original.

sources.quote: q = clip(round(x / s) + z, qmin, qmax)     x̂ = s × (q − z). s > 0 is the step size. z is the integer code for zero. x̂ approximates x.

concepts.title: Selecting quantization ranges, scales, and zero-points
concepts.summary: Choose a bit width and integer code range, then select a real range [a,b] that includes zero using weight statistics or representative activation samples; min/max is a starting point, while percentile or error-based clipping may help. For asymmetric quantization, s = (b − a)/(qmax − qmin) and z = clip(round(qmin − a/s), qmin, qmax). For symmetric signed 4-bit quantization, the example uses codes [−7,7], s = max(|a|,|b|)/7, and z = 0, leaving storage code −8 unused. The examples reconstruct 1.3 as 1.5 (absolute error 0.20) and 0.74 as 0.8 (absolute error 0.06); reconstruction requires the scale and zero-point.

sources.quote: Asymmetric s = (b − a) / (qmax − qmin); z = clip(round(qmin − a / s), qmin, qmax). Symmetric A = max(|a|, |b|); s = A / 7; z = 0 (4-bit example).
Absolute errors are 0.20 and 0.06. Reconstructing either value requires its scale and zero-point.

concepts.title: How outliers affect quantization error
concepts.summary: A single symmetric 4-bit scale spanning values from −0.4 to 7.0 is set by the outlier: A = 7.0 and s = 1.0. That preserves the value 7.0 but maps the four ordinary values to zero, illustrating how an outlier can make one shared scale too coarse and how clipping trades error in one part of the range for error elsewhere.

sources.quote: The outlier preserves its value, while four ordinary weights collapse to zero. Clipping trades one error for another.

concepts.title: Groupwise symmetric INT4 quantization
concepts.summary: Symmetric INT4 stores weights as 4-bit integer values produced by rounding to the nearest even value. Using different scales for smaller groups lets each group adapt to its local value range, but adds scale metadata and requires inference-kernel support. The example shows 128 weights occupying 64 bytes, with one FP16 scale adding 2 bytes (3.1%) before other metadata.

sources.quote: For 128 weights, 4-bit values occupy 64 bytes. One FP16 scale adds 2 bytes, or 3.1%, before zero-points and other metadata.

concepts.title: Precision loss in accumulation and mixed precision
concepts.summary: In the illustrated sum, FP16 spacing at 2048 is 2, so adding 1 and rounding after each step leaves the value at 2048, while summing FP16 inputs in FP32 preserves the increments. Higher precision for sums, normalization, and softmax can limit further error, but upcasting cannot recover bits already lost. Storage and computation may use different precisions; examples include INT4 weights with FP16 activations and FP8 weights with selected components kept in BF16.

sources.quote: Qwen2-7B-Instruct-AWQ INT4 linear weights with FP16 activations. Qwen3-30B-A3B-FP8 FP8 weights, with routers and LM head kept in BF16.

concepts.title: Post-training quantization and quantization-aware training
concepts.summary: Post-training quantization (PTQ) converts an existing trained checkpoint using weight statistics and, for methods such as GPTQ or AWQ, representative calibration inputs. Quantization-aware training (QAT) simulates quantize-and-dequantize operations during the forward pass, updates weights with gradients, and exports low-bit weights after training or fine-tuning; rounding commonly uses an approximate backward gradient such as a straight-through estimator. PTQ is described as a low-cost first deployment candidate, whereas QAT adds training cost to help recover quality.

sources.quote: PTQ is a low-cost first deployment candidate. QAT adds training cost to help recover quality.

concepts.title: Common quantization methods and their mechanisms
concepts.summary: RTN is a PTQ baseline that rounds values to a chosen grid. GPTQ uses calibration inputs and curvature information to reduce layer-output error; AWQ uses activation statistics to rescale important weight channels; and SmoothQuant moves activation outliers into weights so both can use INT8. QAT instead learns with simulated quantization error before conversion. FP8 and FP4 are formats, while PTQ and QAT describe how a quantized model is produced.

sources.quote: FP8 / FP4 are formats. PTQ / QAT describe how a quantized model is produced.
Simulate quantize + dequantize in the forward pass, then update weights with gradients.

concepts.title: Quantization tradeoffs in speed, storage, and quality
concepts.summary: Quantization can affect inference throughput, stored tensor payload, and task scores differently. In the stated single-A100 Qwen2 benchmark, GPTQ INT4 had higher throughput and a smaller payload than BF16, but a lower mean evaluation score; AWQ INT4 had a similar payload and score to GPTQ INT4 but different throughput. Payload includes stored tensor bytes, including scales and unquantized tensors, excludes runtime memory, and quality is measured separately. These are historical results for the specified setup.

sources.quote: Payload = bytes of stored tensors, including scales and unquantized tensors. ... Historical results. Payload excludes runtime memory. Quality uses separate task evaluations.

concepts.title: Scaled dot-product multi-head attention computation
concepts.summary: Multi-head attention computes scores as S = QKᵀ/√dₕ, forms attention weights A = softmax(S + M), and combines values as C = AV. In the illustrated T = 16 case, each head has a 16 × 16 score matrix, with each row comparing one query against all keys. The recap gives the attention FLOP count as 2BT²d and notes that Q and K include RoPE.

concepts.title: Causal masking restricts attention to the prefix
concepts.summary: The causal mask permits query position i to attend to keys at positions j ≤ i by setting M[i,j] = 0, and excludes future positions j > i by setting M[i,j] = −∞ before softmax. Consequently, each query combines information only from its prefix.

sources.quote: M[i,j] = 0 when j ≤ i; M[i,j] = −∞ when j > i. Each query combines only its prefix.
Add M before softmax to hide future positions.

concepts.title: Prompt prefill processes known positions together
concepts.summary: During prefill, all prompt positions are already known, so their causal-attention rows can run together. The final prompt row supplies the last prompt token’s hidden state, which a vocabulary projection uses to predict the first generated token. In the example, the prompt “The sky is” is processed together to select “blue.”

sources.quote: All prompt positions are already known, so their rows can run together. The final row provides the last token’s hidden state. A vocabulary projection predicts the next token.
Prefill The sky is Positions 1–3 together blue (position 4).

source.quote: The quantization and reconstruction equations define q, s, and z; parameter selection then specifies the bit width, integer range, real range, scale, and zero-point.
One symmetric 4-bit scale for all five values: A = 7.0; s = 7.0 / 7 = 1.0; z = 0.
